page.title: I/O processors
page.description: Charts send events to I/O processors, objects of your own that do the I/O and send the answers back as events.

hero.headline: Do a chart's I/O in your own code.
hero.lede: The host does no I/O. A chart sends an event to an I/O processor, an object of yours that does the work and answers with an event.

section.heading: Charts send their requests as events.
section.p: An actor cannot reach the network, a file or a database itself. When a chart needs something from outside, it sends an event to an I/O processor.
Your processor does the work and, if there is an answer, sends it back as an event. The chart says what happens, and your code decides how.

section.heading: Give each processor a type.
section.p: The host's ioProcessors option names the processors its charts may send to, each under a type: any URI you choose.
A processor is an object whose receive(send) the host calls for each send to its type. Its optional location is what the chart reads in _ioprocessors[type].location.
A class instance serves as well as a literal: receive is called as its method, so this is the processor.

example.code: urn:example:prices: lookup tea for session 1 tea costs 4 EUR (answer to ask-1)

section.p: A chart that sends to a type no processor serves gets error.execution. A plain function in place of the object is a TypeError at new Host, naming its type.

section.heading: The send describes one <send>.
section.p: The argument of receive holds the fields of one <send>, read on first access.

row.cell: the host the send came from
<send target> as a string, undefined when it has none

<send id>, or the id the host generated; undefined when it has none. A generated id is unique in the sender's session only (each session's first is send.1), so key what you keep by both: `${send.session}:${send.sendid}`
the <param>s as an object, or the <content>'s value
the sending step's trace as W3C text, undefined when untraced ()
the outgoing half, for a transport ()

section.p: A handler calls at most one of the send's two methods:

item.text: Sends event back to the sender, with this send's sendid as its _event.sendid. The options are traceparent (the answer continues the send's trace unless you give another, or null for a new one), origin (the answer's _event.origin) and raw (the message as you read it, for a chart that wants it).
Gives the sender error.communication with this send's sendid, for a request that could not be done.

section.p: A second answer, or an answer after fail(), throws TA_ERROR_STATE. A handler may also answer nothing: the send was a notification, or the chart waits for a timeout of its own.
The fields origin and message, and the answer's origin and raw, follow the wire format. They serve a processor that carries sends out of the process or speaks SCXML's BasicHTTP ().
The send is a view of the host's memory, valid while the handler runs. Read after the handler returned, it throws TA_ERROR_STALE, so copy what you keep for later.

section.heading: Return a promise to answer later.
section.p: A handler that returns a promise has its send filled with every field before the host moves on. Its answer() and fail() then work whenever the promise gets there, while the host is open.
Until then the actor goes on with its other events, and the answer arrives as an event like any other.
If the sender ended meanwhile, answer() and fail() deliver nothing and return false, and true when the sender gets the event.
Any other refusal still throws: a second answer or a closed host (TA_ERROR_STATE), or data the value table cannot hold.
await host.idle() waits for the host and for the promise the handler returned, so it resolves once the answer ran. A promise the handler starts and does not return is not waited for.
The pending timeout keeps the process alive until host.close().

section.heading: Settle a session's requests when it ends.
section.p: An actor that reaches a top-level <final> ends at once, and SCXML drops the events still in its queue.
So a request queued with actor.send behind the event that ends the actor is lost, and no handler is called.
Let the chart say so first: its <final>'s <onentry> sends to your processor. The handler then settles everything it still holds for that session.

section.heading: A handler that throws fails its send.
section.p: A handler that throws before it answered, or whose promise rejects before it answered, has its send failed. The sender gets error.communication.
An error after the answer fails nothing, and the answer stands. The error itself is reported after the turn, to the first of these:

item.text: the host's onHandlerError(error, effect), when it has one, with the send as effect;
a waiting host.idle(), which rejects with it;
the runtime, as an uncaught exception, or as an unhandled rejection for a promise that rejected.

example.code: the chart got error.communication for g1 idle() rejected: connection refused

section.p: The chart handled error.communication in the same turn, and the error came out of idle() at its end.

section.heading: A handler may call the host.
section.p: Through send.host a handler may send an event to any actor, spawn one or terminate one. send.sender.send(...) sends to the sender.
The input applies at once, and the actors it concerns run in the same or a later turn.
A handler never takes the host's effects, so it has nothing to drain or acknowledge. When it returns, the host goes on.

section.heading: Start lasting actors with a Spawner.
section.p: SCXML has no element that starts an actor which outlives its state: <invoke> stops its child when the state is left.
The package's Spawner is an I/O processor that does it. Give it to the host under a type you choose, and a chart sends it { chart, name, params }.
The host spawns the chart's current version under the name. The sender gets spawned with { name, address } and the send's sendid.
The address is what the sender sends to from then on. A chart the host does not have, or data of another shape, gives the sender error.communication instead.

example.code: room about tea got hello 1 room

section.heading: Give each name one owner.
section.p: The Spawner spawns and does not look names up. One collection actor decides which actors of a kind exist, and only it spawns those names.
A workspace spawns its rooms, for one (the application routes it).
As one actor, it makes one request at a time and records each, so it never asks twice for a name.
The chat-rooms example's workspace keeps a creating table keyed by the spawn's sendid. An entry stays until spawned or error.communication answers it.
Two actors spawning one name is a design error in the application. The core's answer is defined, but it is not what the application meant.
Within one version the oldest holder keeps the name, and a newer version's holder wins (ta_host_actor_by_name in the core's host.h).

section.heading: Deploy a version under an existing name.
section.p: A new version of a chart is a new image: compile it and give it to host.addImage. Adding it is the deploy.
New actors of the chart start in the newest version, running ones finish on theirs, and nothing moves unless asked. The versions need not be compatible (versions and segments).
An actor found by name updates the same way: its owner spawns the new version under the existing name.
From then on the name finds the new actor (@room.acme.general, host.actor('room.acme.general')), since names are looked up newest version first.
The old actor keeps its session, so its session address still reaches it. It runs on its version until it ends.

example.code: room.acme.general runs version 1 room.acme.general runs version 2 room.acme.general runs version 1

section.p: A long-lived actor that must not wait for its end to change, such as a workspace, is moved instead.
host.migrate({ chart: 'workspace' }) moves the running actors to the new version ().
